title: Leap Life
summary: Saul Williams discusses Leap Life, collaboration with Carlos Niño, political histories and using the human voice as a primary instrument. He reflects on the ideas and collaborative work behind his first solo album in more than a decade.
transcript:
Saul Williams spoke with Lauren Taylor about Leap Life, his new album made with Carlos Niño. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 3 September 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: It was a real honour to chat recently with the legendary Saul Williams, who was here in Melbourne in June for Rising, playing shows with his longtime collaborator Carlos Niño and friends. He was also part of Day Tripper, and gave a deep listening and talk session for The Vinyl Factory: Reverb at ACMI. It’s really hard to put a label on Saul Williams. He’s a true renaissance man, a multidisciplinary artist balancing so many creative roles: music, writing and poetry, filmmaking and, of course, acting, most recently in his critically acclaimed role as the preacher Jedidiah Moore in the film Sinners. For nearly three decades, he’s operated at the intersection of language and rhythm. He’s a true icon of spoken word who really helped put slam poetry on the map, and he’s been shattering the boundaries of poetry, punk, hip-hop and political resistance throughout his career. His voice has been a real force for political activism and systematic critique.

His new project, Leap Life, pushes that even further. It operates on the core philosophy that the voice is the instrument, expanding what the definition of music itself can be, and what it means to trust the moment. It sees him working again with Carlos Niño, with a really stacked line-up of guests, including Gonjasufi, Georgia Anne Muldrow, Jimetta Rose, Kamasi Washington, Robert Del Naja, 3D from Massive Attack, Moor Mother and many others. The title comes from Saul’s own leap year birthday: he was born on the 29th of February, so technically he’s only 13 years old, having had 13 official birthdays. So it feels incredibly intentional that the album has 13 songs, each holding a completely different worldview. Saul has described Leap Life not as a conventional studio album, but as a gathering of spirits, histories, frequencies and unfinished revolutions. So I began by asking how he captured that energy, and whether the recording process felt more like an archive or a seance.

Saul: It definitely had a certain type of seance energy, only in that things were aligned so smoothly. It felt as if there were forces at work in putting together this album. I hadn’t really thought very thoroughly beforehand about putting together an album. The album came together through Carlos’s enthusiasm and insistence that it was time. And I went into the studio kind of fresh, with a bunch of music that I’d made, but with no lyrics attached, and just went in there and knocked it out.

Lauren: You mentioned Carlos, who you toured with here. You’ve had a really long working relationship with Carlos Niño as your percussionist and producer, and he’s been named as a musical architect, sequencing your new record too. Can you tell me about your relationship with Carlos? It seems like a very important one in your life.

Saul: Yeah. Actually, the first time I was ever flown to LA to perform, it was by Carlos. That was when my first single or EP came out, on Big Dada, which was over 20 years ago. That’s how we met. It was that night, at the show with Carlos, that I ended up meeting my first producer, Rick Rubin, and a bunch of things that turned into this career happened after that first meeting. So we’d worked together in a promotional capacity before: he would put on shows, what have you. That was a creative capacity, but we hadn’t worked together in a music studio.

A little over a year ago, we decided we were going to work together, and that we would announce we were going into the studio to work on Leap Life. In order to announce that, we put together a concert. That concert became our last album, the TreePeople album, which was not intended as an album. It was just a show to announce that we were going into the studio to work on this album, Leap Life.

Lauren: Perhaps beginning with the title itself, Leap Life points directly to your own leap year birthday, which is so rare: it happens once every four years. Do you feel like you’ve got a unique relationship with time in that way?

Saul: A hundred per cent. When you have a birthday like that, you begin by asking, well, why don’t I have a birthday this year? Who created the calendar? Who created the — whose practice of time are we practising? What do you mean, the Gregorian calendar? Who’s Gregory? Who’s Pope Gregory? Why would the church determine that? All of this stuff. So, of course, it began a long process of questioning. And those questions do have answers.

And when you learn the distinctions between our calendar and, let’s say, many indigenous calendars, where there are 13 moons in a cycle, and 28 days, calendars that perhaps feel way more connected to nature as we know it, which is the root of what we call biodynamics and what have you, you realise that the calendar sometimes feels like an act of disassociation: it separates us from a true understanding of nature and aligns us more with the empire. So it’s August, and you have Augustus. And what does that have to do with anything, other than those who once ruled?

Lauren: In preparing for this interview, I realised I’d never really considered why leap years exist. Obviously they keep our clocks aligned with the Earth’s orbit. Do you see Leap Life as a tool for realigning the human perspective, perhaps?

Saul: I like that idea. Conceptual. But yeah, that is the goal. The realigning that has to occur now: obviously, there are forces at work to maintain a sort of sociopolitical alignment with colonialism and acts of the past. You have a lot of people in power who are focused on keeping things a particular way. And yes, the power of music, which has always been born of ceremony, and has always been used to mobilise, does have that power to realign, and to remind us of our power as people, as listeners, to harmonise, to be a threat to power. So, yeah, that energy is certainly in Leap Life.

Lauren: This new record expands on what the definition of music itself can be, operating on the philosophy that the voice is the instrument. The vocal focus also feels, as you were saying, deeply ceremonial, with a real spiritual invocation. How do you view the relationship between the voice as a tool for political agitation and as a vessel for a more spiritual realm?

Saul: Those two are connected. Those are not separate ideas; it’s the same idea. It’s really just the realisation of what one’s voice is connected to. And with that realisation comes an understanding, perhaps, of, I mean, responsibility sounds like a heavy word, but I do think that those in power, like in the US, where I’m from, for example, who throw around words like freedom, use those words to avoid talking about their responsibilities.

So I think a voice obviously can do a lot. When we sing, there’s so much power and beauty in singing. The voice reflects the possibilities of humanity, not only through the sounds we make, but through the meaning we’re able to emit. Some voices are used manipulatively. And I think there’s also a role for the voice to play in working not to be manipulative, but to open up something, or to remind someone of something. I think there are spiritual and political aspects to that, and they’re intertwined.

Lauren: You said recently that we need our discontent to be voiced, that we need that type of energy on our airwaves right now. What do you think happens to a society when its collective discontent is systematically quietened or filtered out?

Saul: Well, when it’s quietened or filtered out, I think we begin to make a series of mistakes, or what have you. But essentially art, music, entertainment becomes just that: entertainment. It becomes something that’s there to escape, to distract. It ceases to be a threat to power. It serves as an arm of state propaganda, of capitalism. None of these things are crucial to art. Art, theatre and music have disrupted society in the past, have reminded people of what they’re capable of. You think of a play like Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, and the role of Mark Antony’s speech there, which he has to give after promising those in power, who’ve just murdered their leader, that he won’t say anything against them. So he has to find a very careful way of reminding the people that they have power.

There’s a certain tendency that we have. It’s not like we want to fight, or we want to mobilise, or we want to have to overthrow, but there are times when you must, when we can’t allow things to continue the way they are, right? At that moment, it becomes all of our responsibility to do everything within our power, within our reach, to shift things. So if you’re a DJ, you have stuff to play. If you’re a musician, you have music to make. If you’re a teacher, you have stuff you need to instil in students. It doesn’t matter what your lane is, there’s a way in which it plays out.

Lauren: Saul has said that making music is an act of daily necessity for him, and has described the process as a way of both zoning out and zoning in. I asked him how making music allows him to detach from the noise of the world while sharpening his focus.

Saul: Well, typically, whether I’m reading or writing or just living my life in whatever capacity, I’m listening to music. It’s there. Music is there. And there are times when you’re kind of searching for something, whether it’s sonically or energetically. A lot of times I turn to music in those moments, whether it’s music I’ve made or not. Most times it’s music I’ve not made, music by others that I’m listening to. But there are times when even that music doesn’t touch the thing I’m trying to touch. That’s when I end up diving into creating sounds, or exploring sounds, in order to achieve just an idea. It may be for four or five minutes, it may be for five hours. But the ideas begin to accumulate.

And yes, it is part of a kind of creative ecosystem, because it’s one thing to be searching for words. It’s another thing to be searching for sounds, beyond or within a so-called kind of silence: silence in that I’m not using words. So I’m speaking about the process of music instrumentally, initially, for me. Usually when I’m writing a song, I start with music, and eventually words will come. As I was describing earlier with the recording of this album, I started composing a lot of the music, but not with an album in mind. It’s just kind of filling a space. And yeah, it does feed something, but not to the point where it elicited me putting words to it. Some of the music that’s on that album, I sat with literally for years without words. It was not until that brief moment in the studio with Carlos that I decided I was ready to put words to those songs.

Lauren: You have so many incredible collaborators on Leap Life: Kamasi Washington, Georgia Anne Muldrow, Gonjasufi, Moor Mother and, of course, Robert Del Naja, 3D from Massive Attack, who were in Australia recently doing some really incredible shows. I understand Robert gifted you some soundscapes on this new record. Can you tell that story?

Saul: Robert and I have been exchanging music and musical ideas for years. We’ve been exchanging files. We even have an album, Robert, me and Gonjasufi, that’s never been released.

Lauren: Amazing. Can you put that out, please?

Saul: I want to. I can’t wait until we get — So that process with Robert started over a decade ago. Since then, whenever we have something we want to share, we just share it. So some mornings I wake up with a surprise email like, yo, I was thinking of you, check this out. That happened, not so recently, with a bunch of sounds he’d been playing with, and he was like, feel free to play with these if it comes up. So there are three songs on Leap Life from stuff that Robert sent me, that I either began to play with and chop up and add sounds to, or that I used exactly as he sent.

Those songs are ‘Controlled Is Not Controllable’, ‘I Think I Get It Now’ and ‘Not Everything For Sale’. So Robert played a part. Gonjasufi played a part. Like you said, Moor Mother, Kamasi Washington, Jimetta Rose. These are all friends. It’s really like, if I were to piece together an army of people that I trust and have worked with, this is them.

Lauren: There’s also a new book you’ve announced, coming out very soon, called Songs My Mother Taught Me: Why the Artist Must Take Sides, which is about your relationship to politics. Is that correct?

Saul: It’s about my relation to politics and, I guess, in a more general sense, how I’ve grown to relate art to politics. It’s kind of my response to the question, what radicalised you? Basically, last year, 2025, probably around the month of February, after already two years of witnessing all of the horrors that all of us across the world have been witnessing, led by Western government, I decided it was time to shift gears. Aside from the importance of doing what we can from our positions to boost Palestinian voices, and trying to recapture the algorithm, so to speak, to make sure that things aren’t covered up or what have you, I felt it was time to shift gears towards the practices I know best and trust, which, of course, are music, poetry and performance. So between March and August of last year, I recorded Leap Life and I wrote Songs My Mother Taught Me.

We’ve discussed Leap Life, and that’s one aspect of a kind of process for me. And writing Songs My Mother Taught Me, I didn’t really know how this book would come out. I just knew I had to get these ideas out, because I was being asked repeatedly, what do you think is the role of an artist during this time? And I’m no philosopher or what have you, but I can tell the story of how I came to see my role as an artist. That’s what Songs My Mother Taught Me is about.

Lauren: My final question for you, Saul: you’ve stated that you don’t really fuck with hope, and you’ve cited the Audre Lorde poem where she writes that hope is counter-revolutionary. In that way, do you see hope as more of a passive thing? And if so, what sort of active force replaces it for you when you’re creating?

Saul: To clarify, I do think that hope serves a purpose. It’s nice to have a sense of hope, and to be able to trust that the process, that your work, that your vision is not in vain, or our vision of humanity and what we’re working for, the kind of world we want to see, that this work is not in vain, and that we have the potential to transform society and transform ourselves. However, I have an album that came out in 2008 called The Inevitable Rise and Liberation of NiggyTardust! And the word inevitable was always the key word for me, although the public always fixated on NiggyTardust. It’s the inevitable that was crucial in my understanding. For example, some would say that socialism is the science of life: that the only way we can progress as humanity is through reminding ourselves of our relationship to nature, of the responsibilities we have to each other, and making sure that our societies represent us, all of us, properly.

That we don’t extract so much from the earth that we extract ourselves; that we find the balance. And I believe that’s a balance we have to achieve together. So I’ve never really understood the process of what we’re fighting for as something we have to put our hope towards. Yes, there are active ingredients, right? It’s the active ingredients of hope: the ones that contain work, the ones that contain study, the ones that contain organising, the ones that contain focus. Yes, it also embodies play and dance and all of these things. We look at the dance floor as a battlefield, or as a training ground. These are all necessary aspects of what it means to be alive, as is love, and making love, and all of these things. They all play crucial parts in our evolution, in understanding what love is in its broadest sense.

But I’ve just felt there’s a way in which some people lean on hope that is maybe unhealthy. And I’ve never really thought of the process of Black and Indigenous liberation as something rooted in hope. It’s rooted in an inevitability, because if we don’t shift our relationship to each other, to the land, what have you, we’ll be forced to live under the rule of all of the dudes that none of us can stand. The Peter Thiel, I’m blanking on the other guy’s name, the Tesla guy, which is funny. I never blank on his name, but I’m happy to.

Lauren: Elon Musk.

Saul: Yes, and the leadership, and all the hypocrisy that we see. We all see it. We all clearly see all of the evil hypocrisy that we live under, right? And yes, there is an inevitability that comes with the fact that we are not going to be able to sustain a relationship to power as long as power is in hands such as those. So there is an inevitability in it, and it has nothing to do with hope. It has more to do with their projection of, or belief in, our hopelessness: that we will be forced to be surveilled, controlled, and there’s nothing we can do about it.

Lauren: Well, thank you so much, Saul, for being so generous with your time today, and congratulations on Leap Life. It’s an incredible record. I’m very much looking forward to that Gonjasufi, 3D and Saul Williams record coming out soon.

Saul: Thank you. I can’t wait for people to hear it.
